title: By Doing Just Actions We Come to Be Just
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from The Nicomachean Ethics of Aristotle (Project Gutenberg edition).
body: Again, in whatever cases we get things by nature, we get the faculties first and perform the acts of working afterwards; an illustration of which is afforded by the case of our bodily senses, for it was not from having often seen or heard that we got these senses, but just the reverse: we had them and so exercised them, but did not have them because we had exercised them. But the Virtues we get by first performing single acts of working, which, again, is the case of other things, as the arts for instance; for what we have to make when we have learned how, these we learn how to make by making: men come to be builders, for instance, by building; harp-players, by playing on the harp: exactly so, by doing just actions we come to be just; by doing the actions of self-mastery we come to be perfected in self-mastery; and by doing brave actions brave.

And to the truth of this testimony is borne by what takes place in communities: because the law-givers make the individual members good men by habituation, and this is the intention certainly of every law-giver, and all who do not effect it well fail of their intent; and herein consists the difference between a good Constitution and a bad.

So too then is it with the Virtues: for by acting in the various relations in which we are thrown with our fellow men, we come to be, some just, some unjust: and by acting in dangerous positions and being habituated to feel fear or confidence, we come to be, some brave, others cowards.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, in cases where we get things by nature, in what order do we acquire faculties versus performing acts of working?
options: We get the faculties first and perform the acts of working afterwards
We perform the acts of working first and get the faculties afterwards
Faculties and acts of working always appear at exactly the same time
The order differs randomly from person to person

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what example does the author use to illustrate getting a faculty before exercising it?
options: Our bodily senses, such as sight and hearing
The skill of playing the harp
The trade of building houses
The virtue of bravery in battle

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how do men come to be builders?
options: By building
By studying architecture books
By watching other builders work
By being born with the skill

questions.prompt: Per the passage, how do men come to be harp-players?
options: By playing on the harp
By listening to harp music
By reading about harp technique
By being taught music theory alone

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do law-givers use to make individual members of a community good men?
options: Habituation
Punishment alone
Wealth and reward
Public praise alone

questions.prompt: Per the passage, in what does the difference between a good Constitution and a bad one consist?
options: Whether the law-giver succeeds or fails at instilling good habits in citizens
The number of laws a Constitution contains
The wealth of the nation that adopts it
The age of the Constitution itself

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say the Virtues are unlike the bodily senses in how they are acquired?
options: With virtues we must first perform the actions before the corresponding quality exists in us, reversing the usual order for natural faculties
Virtues, like the senses, exist in us from birth without any effort
The bodily senses require years of practice to develop fully
Virtues can only be learned by reading philosophical texts

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author compare becoming virtuous to becoming a builder or harp-player?
options: To show that virtue, like a craft or skill, develops through repeated practice rather than existing from birth
To argue that virtue and craftsmanship have nothing meaningful in common
To suggest that only skilled builders can become virtuous
To prove that virtue requires formal schooling in a trade

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: Virtue is formed through the repeated practice of virtuous actions, just as skills and even good citizens are shaped through habituation
Virtue is an inborn trait that cannot be changed through practice
Only law-givers are capable of becoming truly virtuous
Virtue has nothing to do with a person's actions or habits

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does "habituation" mean?
options: The process of forming a habit through repeated practice
A formal law passed by a government
A punishment given for breaking the law
A natural talent present from birth

questions.prompt: According to the passage, by doing what kind of actions do we come to be "just"?
options: Just actions
Actions performed only by law-givers
Actions praised by a community
Actions taught only in schools

questions.prompt: Per the passage, by doing what actions do we come to be "perfected in self-mastery"?
options: The actions of self-mastery
The actions of building
The actions of playing the harp
The actions of law-making

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is described as "the intention certainly of every law-giver"?
options: To make individual members good men by habituation
To collect taxes efficiently from citizens
To punish wrongdoers as severely as possible
To ensure that citizens remain wealthy

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what do we come to be by acting in dangerous positions and being habituated to feel fear or confidence?
options: Some brave, others cowards
All equally fearless
All equally fearful
Neither brave nor cowardly

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author bring up law-givers and communities right after discussing how individuals form habits?
options: To extend the same principle from individuals to society, showing law-givers deliberately use habituation to shape citizens' character
To argue that communities have no influence on individual virtue at all
To show that law-givers are exempt from needing good habits themselves
To prove that virtue can only be taught by law-givers, never by parents

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what the passage says about becoming just or unjust?
options: We become just or unjust through how we habitually act toward other people in our various relations
Justice is decided entirely at birth and cannot change
Only law-givers can determine who is just or unjust
Justice depends solely on wealth and social status

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean to be "habituated" to feel fear or confidence?
options: To become accustomed to a feeling through repeated experience
To feel a sudden, single, unexpected emotion
To be permanently unable to feel any emotion
To be legally required to feel a certain way
